chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
title: Keg goes to Minneapolis; Lester Young arrives with the Blue Devils
summary: Keg writes about a sax player named Lester Young; the Blue Devils come to Kansas City with Lester, whom Budd compares to Trumbauer.

bands.name: Jesse Stone and His Blue Serenaders

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Well, during that time, along then in the town was Walter Paige and his Blue Devils, and when he came in town he had this sax@phone player which my brother had been writing to me. My brother and I had separated by this time.
Because we don't have your separation.
Oh, you separated in Kansas City.

We separated in Kansas City. He left Jesse STone's band, because the band broke up. We were stranded, we had to go on our own ways, and he went to Minneapolis, Minnesota and joined Eli Rice's band. And of course we kept in touch, close contact with each other, and he wrote me one time and he said, 'Man, there's a sax@phone player playing up here in a little place called The Nest, in Minneapolis, and his name is Lester Young.' He said this cat sounds something like you, and he sure can play. You've got to hear him.
So I had never heard Lester, so as I'm saying, finally, one day in come the Blue Devils. Of all of the guys I knew, but now they had with them this tenor sax@phone
Well Keg wasn't with the Blue Devils then, was he?

No, no. No. See, Keg had been playing up with Eli Rice and Grant Moore out of Milwaukee, and you know, and him and Joe Thomas, trumpet player, Eddie Thompkins, they all played with Eli Rice after they left Jesse Stone, see?

So in walks this guy Lester Young, blowing, and he had -- he was at that time playing two different styles. I feel always felt that Lester was inspired by Frankie Trumbauer. Well he used to play alto, you know. And his style was mixed. At one time he would play a type of Frankie Trumbauer thing, then he would go into his own thing, which made his tone like it was, you know, like he never had the big robust sound that Coleman Hawkins had.

Oh, I skipped how I first met Hawk$. We'll get back to that.
